extracted.intended_audience: conference organizers, peer-review researchers, and ML researchers interested in automated checklist/author-assistant tools
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of an LLM-based assistant that vets conference paper submissions against an author checklist (NeurIPS experiment), including usefulness, accuracy, robustness to gaming, and impact on author revisions. The paper reports an experiment with voluntary submissions, surveys, resubmission analysis, and adversarial tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation against NeurIPS author checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Assistant validates whether papers adhere to the author checklist used by NeurIPS, which includes questions to ensure compliance with research and manuscript preparation standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to vet paper submissions against submission standards; the assistant's role is to check checklist completion and flag non-compliance with research/manuscript-preparation requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived usefulness to authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether authors find the assistant helpful in verifying checklist completion and guiding improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by post-usage surveys: over 70% of authors found the assistant useful; 70% indicated they would revise their papers or checklist responses based on its feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on author behavior / induced revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether feedback from the assistant leads authors to make substantive revisions to submissions or to change checklist responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey responses and analysis of re-submissions indicate authors made substantive revisions in response to specific LLM feedback; however, causal attribution to the assistant is not definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of assistant feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: The correctness and factual reliability of the assistant's outputs when assessing checklist items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the experiment, inaccuracy was the most frequent issue authors flagged (20 out of 52 flagged instances); accuracy is a primary quality criterion for usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration / excessive strictness
rubrics_metrics.description: The assistant's tendency to be overly strict or to over-report non-compliance (sensitivity and thresholding of checks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive strictness was frequently reported (14 out of 52 flagged instances); balancing false positives and false negatives is important for author trust and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness to gaming and fabricated justifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Susceptibility of the assistant to manipulation, e.g., producing fabricated justifications to inflate checklist scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments revealed the assistant could be manipulated to enhance scores through fabricated justifications, highlighting the need for defenses, verification, and adversarial testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation methodology and deployment metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate metrics and experimental design for assessing such assistants, including voluntary submission uptake, post-usage surveys, re-submission analysis, and adversarial/gaming experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 234 papers voluntarily submitted to the assistant in the NeurIPS experiment; combine quantitative adoption/usage statistics with surveys and resubmission comparisons to assess impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of causal attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that observed improvements or changes cannot always be definitively attributed to the assistant alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes causal attribution to the assistant is not definitive and relies on qualitative evidence; evaluations should account for confounders and use careful study designs when possible.
